segments.narration: Teddy bears left in this English spring acquire a hard stone exterior. In Knaresborough, North Yorkshire, hanging a soft toy under dripping water coats it in minerals within months.
Victorian top hats, teacups, and boots left beneath the cascade all suffered the exact same fate. Historically, frightened locals avoided touching the water, convinced the spring was cursed.
segments.visual_query: victorian items stone petrified water cavern

segments.narration: Was this real black magic freezing ordinary objects in time? Legend claimed the cave was birthed by a medieval prophetess, leaving behind water that turned anything to stone.
The truth came when scientists analyzed the spring's chemical makeup. The water originates deep underground, dissolving high concentrations of calcite and rich minerals from ancient limestone rock.
segments.visual_query: underground limestone water spring cave geological

segments.narration: As water drips and evaporates, heavy mineral deposits build up layer by layer, encasing objects in a hard calcite shell. Since the shell seals out air and prevents organic decay, could an item preserved here survive for thousands of years?
segments.visual_query: calcite mineral spring rock formation dripping

accuracy_flags.claim: Objects hung under the dripping water at the Petrifying Well in Knaresborough turn to solid mineral stone within months.
accuracy_flags.note: The narration claims objects turn to solid stone and transform into rock, but the reference explicitly states that objects in petrifying wells merely acquire a stony mineral exterior overlaid on top, rather than undergoing true petrification where the constituent molecules are replaced by stone.
